title: Runtime change impact brief — flash attention + paged KV + continuous batching
content:
Summary:
This brief summarizes a set of end-to-end onboarding evaluations run after enabling two runtime changes together: the new FlashAttention codepath, the paged KV cache allocator, and a modified continuous-batching scheduler (batching window reduced from 12ms -> 6ms). We observed mixed outcomes: meaningful cost/throughput improvements on long-token streaming flows, but a reproducible quality regression on multi-turn QA prompt sets and a p95 tail latency increase for small-batch low-latency routes.

Background & motivation:
- Goal: reduce per-token compute cost and improve throughput for high-concurrency customers while keeping quality and latency SLOs.
- Change set tested together:
  * FlashAttention v2 (kernel replacement, lower mem copies for attention)
  * Paged KV cache (sharded/paged allocation to reduce memory pressure on large context)
  * Continuous batching: narrower micro-batching window to prioritize latency for interactive flows while still allowing batching for throughput
- These were introduced as a combined candidate because they interact (FlashAttention improves long-seq perf; paged KV reduces peak memory allowing larger stable batches; continuous batching window tweak optimizes latency/throughput tradeoff).

Test harness and scope:
- Models: open-model-x-13b (FP16), open-model-x-7b (quantized), small-llm-2.7b (baseline internal).
- Hardware: A100-80GB multi-tenant nodes (hosted) and dedicated rtx-a5000 pools for private deployments.
- Prompt sets:
  1) onboarding-qa-multiturn (350 sessions, avg 6 turns, domain: customer support)
  2) long-doc-summarization (200 prompts, avg 1.2k tokens output)
  3) low-latency-chat (synthetic webchat, 6k short-turn interactions, avg 40 tokens)
  4) code-gen-snippets (unit tests + code completions, 120 prompts)
- Metrics collected: latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), cost-estimated GPU-seconds/token, generation quality: exact-match for QA set, embedding-cosine (instruction similarity), hallucination-rate (manual label sample), avg logprob, and downstream eval win-rate (pairwise A/B on 1k completions).
- Canary run: 72 hours per configuration, repeated 3x across different node pools. Baseline: current runtime (legacy attention, monolithic KV, 12ms batching). Candidate: combined changes.

Key results (aggregate deltas candidate vs baseline):
- Long-doc-summarization: throughput +28% tokens/sec, cost-per-token -18%, quality (ROUGE-L proxy) unchanged (delta +0.6%).
- Code-gen-snippets: throughput +12%, latency p95 -8%, quality (unit-test pass rate) unchanged within noise.
- Low-latency-chat: p95 latency increased from 42ms -> 68ms (+62%), p99 increased more dramatically on small batches; throughput marginally higher but not meaningful for this workload. Observed more queuing microbursts.
- Onboarding QA multi-turn: exact-match fell from 72.3% -> 66.1% (delta -6.2pp), embedding-similarity to gold answers down -3.8 cosine points, hallucination rate (sampled 200 responses) increased from 4.5% -> 9.0%. Win-rate A/B vs baseline: baseline preferred 58% of the time.

Fine-grained observations and possible causes:
1) Multi-turn context degradation (largest user visible regression)
   - Symptom: candidate shows repeated partial answers, truncated entities across turns. Failure concentrated on sessions with >8 turns and many short answers.
   - Hypothesis: paged KV introduces micro-misalignment in KV indexing for KV-cache hits on subsequent turns under the new allocation strategy. FlashAttention changes to attention kernel timing may cause subtle differences in rounding/FP behavior for attention keys/values, amplifying when combined with paged eviction/resharding.
   - Evidence: replaying the same session while toggling only paged KV (keeping FlashAttention off) reduces the exact-match drop by ~60%. Toggling only FlashAttention reduces drop by ~30%.

2) Low-latency p95 increase
   - Symptom: small-batch interactive routes see tail latency spikes.
   - Hypothesis: continuous-batching window shrink interacts poorly with scheduler backpressure on multi-tenant nodes; more frequent smaller batches lead to more kernel launches and some serialization overhead that dominates for very short sequences. Also observed increased context switch overhead on CPU preparation threads.
   - Evidence: CPU-side trace shows increased syscalls per second during candidate runs; synthetic single-tenant runs did not show as large regression (indicates multi-tenant interference).

3) Positive: long-sequence throughput gains
   - Root cause: FlashAttention reduces memory bandwidth and kernel runtime for attention on long sequences. Paged KV lowers OOM/copy stalls enabling higher steady-state throughput.

Actionable triage steps (ordered by risk & ROI):
- Immediate (blocker if customer-facing): roll candidate out to dedicated-only pools where we can control multi-tenancy; revert candidate on shared hosted pool for low-latency routes until tail latency regression understood.
- Short term (next 1 week): reproduce exact-match drop in minimal isolated harness with focused instrumentation of KV indices, and add checksums for KV page boundaries during replay to detect misalignment. Run FlashAttention-only, PagedKV-only, and combined permutations across the failing sessions to isolate amplification.
- Medium term (2–4 weeks): introduce automated canary metric for multi-turn QA: target thresholds exact-match delta > -2pp or hallucination-rate > +2pp triggers rollback. Instrument continuous-batching scheduler to emit batch-size histograms with tenant labels; add kernel launch latency metric.
- Engineering experiments to run in parallel:
  * Increase paging granularity (larger page size) to see if misalignment windows shrink.
  * Add deterministic KV page pinning for the first N turns in a session (prevent eviction for warm sessions).
  * Revisit continuous-batching window (test 8ms, 10ms) and measure p95 under multi-tenant stress.
  * Add an FP-stability run (use deterministic seed and fused kernels disabled) to measure numeric drift introduced by FlashAttention.

Recommended rollout plan:
1) Hold combined change on shared hosted low-latency routes.
2) Deploy combined candidate to dedicated pools where customers can opt-in; monitor the canary metrics granularly for 72 hours.
3) If dedicated pools pass, progressively enable paged KV in shared environments but keep FlashAttention gate closed for multi-tenant low-latency route until numeric stability fixes are verified.
4) After mitigations (KV pinning or page-granularity change) and passing isolated exact-match tests, re-run full canary and use graded percentage rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on metric breach.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Is the multi-turn QA exact-match drop acceptable for early adopter customers on dedicated pools (we can provide a list of impacted customers)? (Decision owner: Product + CS)
- Do we prioritize throughput/cost wins for long-doc workloads at the expense of small interactive p95? Can we offer a per-route runtime policy? (Decision owner: Product + Platform)
- Should we invest in KV-page-level checksums and deterministic pinning as a long-term fix (cost x FTE estimated in linked PR)? (Decision owner: Eng leads + Applied ML)

Logs and artifacts attached:
- PR: https://git.company/repo/pull/8742 (runtime: flash + paged-kv + cont-batching)
- Replay harness: confluence.company/pages/attached/eval-suite-2026-02 (replay config and node manifests)
- Failing session examples: s3://replay-buckets/regressions/qa-multiturn/failing-sessions-2026-03.tar.gz

Appendix: quick checklist for next 48h:
- [ ] Run FlashAttention-only and PagedKV-only permutations on failing sessions with high-fidelity traces (owner: Marcus).
- [ ] Add KV page boundary checksum to replay harness and run 1k session sweep (owner: Tomás).
- [ ] Reconfigure continuous-batching window to 8ms on a small canary (owner: Eleni).
- [ ] Prepare customer communication for dedicated-only opt-in with known risks (owner: CS lead).

Notes: this brief is written for technical stakeholders (applied ML, infra, product) to decide on immediate rollout guardrails. The underlying regressions appear to be an interaction effect — isolating the paging behavior is highest ROI for restoring QA quality while preserving throughput gains on long-doc workloads.
